analysis.one_liner: Caps commercials in children's TV at roughly 10 to 12 minutes per hour and funds educational children's programming.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed the Children's Television Act by voice vote in July 1990, but the House never voted on the Senate bill; the same rules moved ahead through the House companion, H.R. 1677.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill told the Federal Communications Commission to write rules limiting how many commercials can run in children's television programs — 10.5 minutes per hour on weekends and 12 on weekdays. It also required the FCC to look at whether stations serve children's educational needs when deciding whether to renew their broadcast licenses. A second title created a National Endowment for Children's Educational Television, giving federal grants to producers of educational shows for kids, with public television getting first airing rights for two years.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and parents, who would get fewer commercials during children's programming and stations with a renewal-time obligation to serve kids' educational needs. Producers of educational children's television would gain a new federal grant source.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children, parents, and educational TV producers

how_it_helps.text: Caps advertising in children's television programming at 10.5 minutes per hour on weekends and 12 minutes per hour on weekdays.

Requires the FCC, when reviewing a station's license renewal application, to consider whether the station complied with the ad limits and served the educational and informational needs of children through its programming.

Creates a National Endowment for Children's Educational Television under the Secretary of Education to make grants for shows that build children's fundamental intellectual skills, with grants capped at 75 percent of project cost and $10 million authorized for fiscal year 1991.

Gives programming funded by the Endowment an exclusive two-year first-run window on public and noncommercial television, after which commercial stations and cable systems may air it so long as they run it without commercial interruption.

analysis.who_pays: Broadcasters and advertisers, who would sell fewer commercial minutes during children's programs, and taxpayers, who would fund the Endowment's grants.

drawbacks.text: The caps still allow more than ten minutes of advertising per hour in children's programming, and after January 1, 1993 the FCC may review and loosen those limits after notice and public comment.
Enforcement is indirect: compliance is weighed when a station's license comes up for renewal rather than backed by automatic fines or penalties.

The Endowment is modest and cost-shared — grants cover at most 75 percent of a project's cost, and only $10 million is authorized for fiscal year 1991 — so the federal push for educational programming would be small relative to the size of children's television.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are real but modest: the ad caps leave considerable commercial time in children's shows, enforcement rides on the license-renewal process rather than penalties, and the new Endowment is small. Still, the bill attacks a genuine problem — heavy advertising aimed at young children and too little educational programming — at low public cost, so the benefits plausibly outweigh the costs.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it by voice vote on July 19, 1990, but the House held the bill at the desk and never voted on it; the Senate record points to the House companion, H.R. 1677, as the vehicle that carried the same children's television rules forward.

narrative.text: Senator Hollings introduced S. 1992 on November 22, 1989, and the Senate Commerce Committee reported the original measure to the Senate the same day, with written report No. 101-227 and minority views filed.
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders the same day it was introduced.
On July 19, 1990, the Senate passed the bill with an amendment by voice vote; the amendment added Title II, the National Endowment for Children's Educational Television.
The Senate's action was sent to the House on July 24, 1990; the House received the bill and held it at the desk, and no House vote on S. 1992 appears in the record before the 101st Congress ended.
On November 8, 1990, the Senate action history notes 'See also H.R. 1677,' the House companion carrying the children's television provisions.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broadcasters and advertisers got a few more months without the advertising caps, since the Senate bill died quietly at the House desk; children's advocates, meanwhile, pursued the identical rules through the House companion H.R. 1677 that the Senate record flags.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Broadcasters, briefly; the rules arrived via H.R. 1677

for.name: Ernest F. Hollings
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-SC); Chairman, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and, as committee chairman, reported the original measure to the Senate with a written report on the same day it was introduced.

for.name: The Senate
for.what_they_did: Passed the bill with an amendment (adding the educational television endowment) by voice vote on July 19, 1990.

against.name: The House
against.what_they_did: Received the Senate bill on July 24, 1990, and held it at the desk; the House never brought S. 1992 to a vote.

against.name: Senate Commerce Committee minority
against.role: Republican members of the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Filed minority views against the committee's report of the original measure.

sides.party_line_note: No recorded votes exist — the Senate passed the bill by voice vote — but the committee's Republican minority filed minority views on the original measure, signaling some Republican reservations, while the House's inaction left the bill's fate unrecorded by party.

industries.note: Stations would have to cut children's advertising to 10.5-12 minutes per hour and face FCC scrutiny of their children's programming at license renewal. Their interest in keeping ad minutes and renewal flexibility ran against the bill's protections for child viewers.
The caps directly reduce the commercial time advertisers can sell to reach child audiences. Fewer ad minutes aimed at children is the bill's central cost to this industry.

industries.industry: Public television and educational programming producers
industries.note: The Endowment would fund production of educational children's shows, with public and noncommercial stations holding exclusive airing rights for the first two years. Producers get a new revenue stream tied to a public good.

The ad limits expressly include cable operators, so cable would bear the same children's advertising caps as broadcasters. On the other side, cable systems could later air Endowment-funded programming for a fee, so long as they run it without commercial interruption.
